key_insight: As the compression-corner angle increases, shock-boundary-layer interaction strengthens dramatically, driving much larger wall-pressure fluctuations and acoustic loading, especially after separation and reattachment.
engineering_relevance: This matters for hypersonic vehicle design because stronger corner angles can sharply amplify unsteady loads, noise, and structural/thermal risk near compression ramps and control surfaces.
method: Large-eddy simulations of a Mach 6.04 hypersonic boundary layer over a compression ramp.
Angles studied: 10°, 20°, 30°, and 34°, covering attached to strongly separated regimes.
Pressure, acoustic-loading, and band-filtered spatio-temporal analyses used to identify where and how fluctuations intensify.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 312% increase in peak RMS wall-pressure fluctuations from R20 to R30, a further 67% increase from R30 to R34, and acoustic loading rising from 140 dB upstream to about 177 dB downstream of reattachment in the 34° case.
watch_item: These results come from a single high-speed flow condition (Mach 6.04, Reθ = 4340), so the observed trends may not generalize without checking other Mach numbers, Reynolds numbers, and geometries.
paper_title: Acoustic Loading Beneath High-Speed Flow Over a Compression Ramp at Different Angles
